analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to get your opt-in consent before collecting, selling, or sharing sensitive personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required opt-in consent for companies using people's sensitive personal data, died in committee without a vote in the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring any company that collects or shares sensitive personal information — health data, financial records, precise location, browsing history, biometrics — to get people's explicit opt-in consent first. Companies would have had to publish clear, readable privacy policies explaining who gets the data and for how long, and large companies would have needed annual independent privacy audits. It also would have let state attorneys general sue violators in federal court. The bill never received a hearing, vote, or any committee action after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users gain a real say over their health, financial, location, and browsing data: nothing could be collected, sold, or shared with third parties unless they explicitly opt in, and they would get plain-language explanations of who takes their data and what happens to it. State attorneys general would gain a new tool to sue companies that misuse data.

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies to get affirmative, express, opt-in consent before collecting, storing, processing, selling, or sharing sensitive personal information such as health records, financial data, precise location, browsing history, and biometrics.

Requires a free, plain-language, prominent privacy and data-use policy that names who is collecting the data, why, who it is shared with, how long it is kept, how consent can be withdrawn, and how data is protected.
Requires large operators to obtain annual privacy audits from independent third-party professionals, with findings available to the FTC and state attorneys general.
Gives state attorneys general power to sue companies in federal court for violations, adding an enforcement channel beyond the FTC.

analysis.who_pays: Large tech platforms, data brokers, and any operator of websites or online services handling sensitive data would bear compliance costs: overhauled consent flows, detailed public privacy policies, and annual third-party privacy audits (companies with 500 or fewer employees are exempt from the audits). Some of that cost could pass through in prices or reduced free services.

drawbacks.text: Companies would face real compliance costs: annual third-party privacy audits for large operators, detailed public privacy policies, and new consent workflows that could slow down services built on data collection.

The bill leaves significant carve-outs: opt-in consent does not apply when processing matches what a 'reasonable user' would expect from the existing relationship, and routine security and fraud uses are exempt, which narrows how much new protection many users would actually notice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — opt-in consent, plain-language disclosures, annual audits, state enforcement — are real and meaningful for anyone whose data is collected. The costs are modest and largely borne by large data-driven firms: compliance and audit expenses, and possibly less free ad-supported service. Exemptions for small businesses and routine operations soften the burden on small firms. On balance, a well-designed bill whose costs fall mostly on companies whose business models rely on collecting sensitive data.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Introduced on September 24, 2018, near the end of the 115th Congress, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action was ever taken: no subcommittee consideration, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting and selling sensitive personal data are better off, since no consent or audit requirements took effect.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three House sponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced far enough for a vote that would reveal the parties' positions. [S4]

industries.note: The bill explicitly covers entities that buy and sell consumer data without direct consumer interaction, and would require opt-in consent before they can use or sell sensitive data, undercutting a business built on trading personal information without asking. [S3]

industries.industry: Internet platforms and online service providers
industries.note: Large platforms would bear audit and compliance costs and could no longer monetize sensitive data by default, but the bill also standardizes rules and exempts companies with 500 or fewer employees from audits. [S3]
Annual independent privacy audits for large operators would create a new market for privacy professionals. [S3]
